# Cardiac Contractility Modulation Therapy for Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Despite substantial advances in pharmacological and device-based therapy, heart failure (HF) remains a major source of morbidity and mortality worldwide [1]. A large proportion of patients with HF and reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) remain symptomatic on optimal medical therapy yet are ineligible for cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) because of a narrow QRS complex—a population estimated to exceed half a million in the United States alone [2]. Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) has emerged as a device-based therapy designed specifically for this gap. CCM signals, consisting of biphasic high-voltage bipolar signals delivered to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period, have been shown to improve symptoms, exercise tolerance and quality of life and reduce the rate of HF hospitalizations in patients with ejection fractions between 25% and 45%. [3]

## Mechanism of Action

Unlike pacing stimuli, CCM signals are nonexcitatory: they are delivered during the absolute refractory period and therefore do not trigger a new action potential. These high-amplitude, biphasic impulses seem to alter intracellular calcium handling, resulting in an increase in myocardial contractility without an associated increase in oxygen consumption. [4] This dissociation between inotropy and oxygen demand distinguishes CCM from classical positive inotropes. The acute effect is rapid; within one beat following initiation of the CCM signal, contractility in isolated rabbit papillary muscle strips increases, but is attenuated as soon as the signal is withdrawn. [5] Beyond acute changes, chronic stimulation appears to drive molecular reverse remodeling. In a study of endomyocardial biopsies, the effects of cardiac contractility modulation electrical signals on expression of fetal, calcium cycling, and stress genes were examined in 11 heart failure patients. [6] Mechanistic reviews summarize that these signals have myocardial effects within minutes to hours including phosphorylation of key proteins involved with calcium cycling and contractile proteins and shifts of myocardial gene expression from a fetal genotype typical of chronic heart failure to a more normal adult genotype, and over weeks to months these effects are evident in regions remote from the stimulation site. [7] Experimentally, the inotropic effect was confirmed to be uncoupled from energetic cost [8], and dedicated mechanistic reviews further elaborate calcium-handling and neurohormonal contributions [9,10].

## Clinical Trial Evidence

The clinical program advanced through the "FIX-HF" series. The FIX-CHF-4 study performed a randomized, double-blind, crossover study of CCM signals in heart failure patients, in which 164 subjects with ejection fraction below 35% and NYHA Class II or III symptoms received a CCM pulse generator. [11] The first large US trial was FIX-HF-5, designed and rationalized in earlier publications [12,13]. CCM was tested in 428 New York Heart Association class III or IV, narrow QRS heart failure patients with ejection fraction ≤35% randomized to optimal medical therapy plus CCM versus OMT alone. [14] The primary end point of an improvement in ventilatory anaerobic threshold was not met; however, the OMT plus CCM group demonstrated improved quality of life, NYHA class, and peak VO2 at 6 months, with comparable mortality and hospitalizations satisfying a prespecified noninferiority safety end point. [14] A prespecified subgroup analysis identified patients with higher ejection fraction as deriving greater benefit [15].

This subgroup signal prompted the confirmatory FIX-HF-5C trial [16]. A total of 160 patients with NYHA functional class III or IV symptoms, QRS duration <130 ms, and ejection fraction ≥25% and ≤45% were randomized to continued medical therapy or CCM for 24 weeks. [17] The investigators concluded that CCM is safe, improves exercise tolerance and quality of life in the specified group of HF patients, and leads to fewer HF hospitalizations. [17] A subsequent study evaluated a simplified two-lead system. Because prior studies of CCM employed a 3-lead Optimizer system, a new 2-lead system eliminated the need for an atrial lead, and this study tested the safety and effectiveness of this 2-lead system compared with the 3-lead system. [18] A key practical consequence was that reliance on ventricular sensing alone allowed CCM to be delivered to patients with atrial fibrillation [19].

## Pooled and Long-Term Data

A patient-level meta-analysis strengthened the efficacy signal. Pooled analysis showed that, compared with control, CCM significantly improved peak VO2, 6-minute walk test distance, and quality of life measured by the MLWHFQ. [20] Observational data have addressed harder outcomes: a multicenter analysis reported that cardiac contractility modulation improves long-term survival and hospitalizations in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. [21] Long-term registry experience with the Optimizer Smart system [22] and single-center cohorts [23] have reported sustained functional and survival benefits, while real-world cohorts confirm improvement in NYHA class and reduced hospitalizations [24]. The therapy received FDA approval in 2019 for symptomatic HFrEF with ejection fraction 25–45% who are not CRT candidates [25].

## Guidelines, Emerging Indications, and Future Directions

CCM is incorporated into contemporary HF guidance, including the 2021 ESC and 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA documents [26,27]. Interest has expanded toward higher ejection fractions. A pilot study aimed to assess the potential benefits of CCM in patients with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). [28] Comprehensive reviews emphasize that benefit appears greatest in patients with LVEF approximately 25–45% spanning HFrEF and HFmrEF [29,30], and that ongoing randomized trials—including dedicated HFmrEF/HFpEF studies and a combined CCM–defibrillator device—will further define the role of this therapy.

## Conclusion

CCM offers a mechanistically distinct, evidence-supported option for symptomatic HFrEF patients with narrow QRS who fall outside CRT indications, improving exercise capacity, quality of life, and hospitalization rates, with emerging data in HFmrEF and HFpEF awaiting confirmation in adequately powered randomized trials.
